{{Short description|Properties linking logical conjunction and disjunction}}
{{Logical connectives sidebar}}
In [[propositional logic]] and [[Boolean algebra]], there is a '''duality between [[Logical conjunction|conjunction]] and [[Logical disjunction|disjunction]]''',<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Duality in Logic and Language {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://iep.utm.edu/duality-in-logic-and-language/ |access-date=2024-06-10 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1.1 Logical Operations |url=https://www.whitman.edu/mathematics/higher_math_online/section01.01.html |access-date=2024-06-10 |website=www.whitman.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Look |first=Brandon C. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NDRuBAAAQBAJ |title=The Bloomsbury Companion to Leibniz |date=2014-09-25 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=978-1-4725-2485-0 |pages=127 |language=en}}</ref> also called the '''duality principle'''.<ref name=":13">{{Cite book |last=Howson |first=Colin |title=Logic with trees: an introduction to symbolic logic |date=1997 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-13342-5 |location=London; New York |pages=41, 44–45}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Boolean algebra, Part 1 {{!}} Review ICS 241 |url=https://courses.ics.hawaii.edu/ReviewICS241/morea/boolean-algebra/readings-boolean-algebra-1.html |access-date=2024-06-10 |website=courses.ics.hawaii.edu}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Kurki-Suonio |first=R. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EvwYxKptVmEC |title=A Practical Theory of Reactive Systems: Incremental Modeling of Dynamic Behaviors |date=2005-07-20 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-540-27348-6 |pages=80–81 |language=en}}</ref> It is the most widely known example of duality in logic.<ref name=":0" /> The duality consists in these [[metalogic]]al theorems:

* In [[Classical logic|classical]] propositional logic, the connectives for [[Conjunction (logic)|conjunction]] and [[Logical disjunction|disjunction]] can be defined in terms of each other, and consequently, only one of them needs to be taken as primitive.<ref name=":13" /><ref name=":0" />
* If <math>\varphi^{D}</math> is used as notation to designate the result of replacing every instance of conjunction with disjunction, and every instance of disjunction with conjunction (e.g. <math>p \land q</math> with <math>q \lor p</math>, or vice-versa), in a given formula <math>\varphi</math>, and if <math>\overline{\varphi}</math> is used as notation for replacing every [[Sentence letter|sentence-letter]] in <math>\varphi</math> with its negation (e.g., <math>p</math> with <math>\neg p</math>), and if the symbol <math>\models</math> is used for semantic consequence and ⟚ for semantical equivalence between logical formulas, then it is demonstrable that <math>\varphi^{D}</math> ⟚ <math>\neg \overline{\varphi}</math>,<ref name=":13" /><ref name=":17">{{Cite book |last=Bostock |first=David |title=Intermediate logic |date=1997 |publisher=Clarendon Press; Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-875141-0 |location=Oxford : New York |pages=62–65}}</ref><ref name=":2" /> and also that <math>\varphi \models \psi</math> if, and only if, <math>\psi^{D} \models \varphi^{D}</math>,<ref name=":17" /> and furthermore that if <math>\varphi</math> ⟚ <math>\psi</math> then <math>\varphi^{D}</math> ⟚ <math>\psi^{D}</math>.<ref name=":17" /> (In this context, <math>\overline{\varphi}^{D}</math> is called the ''dual'' of a formula <math>\varphi</math>.)<ref name=":13" /><ref name=":1" />

== Mutual definability ==
The connectives may be defined in terms of each other as follows:
:<math>\varphi\vee\psi :\equiv\neg(\neg\varphi\and\neg\psi).</math> (1)
:<math>\varphi\and\psi :\equiv \neg(\neg\varphi\vee\neg\psi).</math> (2)
:<math>\neg(\neg\varphi\vee\neg\psi)\equiv\neg\neg(\neg\neg\varphi\and\neg\neg\psi)\equiv\varphi\and\psi.</math> (3)

=== Functional completeness ===
Since the [[Disjunctive normal form|Disjunctive Normal Form Theorem]] shows that the set of connectives <math>\{\and, \vee, \neg\}</math> is [[Functional completeness|functionally complete]], these results show that the sets of connectives <math>\{\and, \neg\}</math> and <math>\{\vee, \neg\}</math> are themselves functionally complete as well.

=== De Morgan's laws ===
[[De Morgan's laws]] also follow from the definitions of these connectives in terms of each other, whichever direction is taken to do it.<ref name=":0" />

:<math>\neg(\varphi\vee\psi)\equiv\neg\varphi\and\neg\psi.</math> (4)

:<math>\neg(\varphi\and\psi)\equiv\neg\varphi\vee\neg\psi.</math> (5)

== Duality properties ==

The ''dual'' of a sentence is what you get by swapping all occurrences of <math display="inline">\vee</math> and <math display="inline">\and</math>, while also negating all propositional constants. For example, the dual of <math display="inline">(A\and B\vee C)</math> would be <math display="inline">(\neg A\vee\neg B\and\neg C)</math>. The dual of a formula <math display="inline">\varphi</math> is notated as <math display="inline">\varphi^*</math>. The ''Duality Principle'' states that in classical propositional logic, any sentence is equivalent to the negation of its dual.<ref name=":13" /><ref name=":17" />

:'''Duality Principle:''' For all <math display="inline">\varphi</math>, we have that <math display="inline">\varphi=\neg(\varphi^*)</math>.<ref name=":13" /><ref name=":17" /> 
:'''Proof:''' By induction on complexity. For the base case, we consider an arbitrary atomic sentence <math display="inline">A</math>. Since its dual is <math display="inline">\neg A</math>, the negation of its dual will be <math display="inline">\neg\neg A</math>, which is indeed equivalent to <math display="inline">A</math>. For the induction step, we consider an arbitrary <math display="inline">\varphi</math> and assume that the result holds for all sentences of lower complexity. Three cases:
:# If <math display="inline">\varphi</math> is of the form <math display="inline">\neg\psi</math> for some <math display="inline">\psi</math>, then its dual will be <math display="inline">\neg(\psi^*)</math> and the negation of its dual will therefore be <math display="inline">\neg\neg(\psi^*)</math>. Now, since <math display="inline">\psi</math> is less complex than <math display="inline">\varphi</math>, the induction hypothesis gives us that <math display="inline">\psi=\neg(\psi^*)</math>. By substitution, this gives us that <math display="inline">\varphi=\neg\neg(\psi^*)</math>, which is to say that <math display="inline">\varphi</math> is equivalent to the negation of its dual.
:# If <math display="inline">\varphi</math> is of the form <math display="inline">(\psi\vee\chi)</math> for some <math display="inline">\psi</math> and <math display="inline">\chi</math>, then its dual will be <math display="inline">(\psi^*\and\chi^*)</math>, and the negation of its dual will therefore be <math display="inline">\neg(\psi^*\and\chi^*)</math>. Now, since <math display="inline">\psi</math> and <math display="inline">\chi</math> are less complex than <math display="inline">\varphi</math>, the induction hypothesis gives us that <math display="inline">\psi=\neg(\psi^*)</math> and <math display="inline">\chi=\neg(\chi^*)</math>. By substitution, this gives us that <math display="inline">\varphi=\neg(\psi^*)\vee\neg(\chi^*)</math> which in turn gives us that <math display="inline">\varphi=\neg(\psi^*\and\chi^*)</math> by [[De Morgan's laws|DeMorgan's Law]]. And that is once again just to say that <math display="inline">\varphi</math> is [[Logical biconditional|equivalent]] to the [[negation]] of its dual.
:# If <math display="inline">\varphi</math> is of the form <math display="inline">\psi\vee\chi</math>, the result follows by analogous reasoning.

=== Further duality theorems ===
Assume <math>\varphi \models \psi</math>. Then <math>\overline{\varphi} \models \overline{\psi}</math> by uniform substitution of <math>\neg P_i</math> for <math>P_i</math>. Hence, <math>\neg \psi \models \neg \varphi</math>, [[Proof by contrapositive|by contraposition]]; so finally, <math>\psi^D \models \varphi^D</math>, by the property that <math>\varphi^{D}</math> ⟚ <math>\neg \overline{\varphi}</math>, which was just proved above.<ref name=":17" /> And since <math>\varphi^{DD} = \varphi</math>, it is also true that <math>\varphi \models \psi</math> if, and only if, <math>\psi^D \models \varphi^D</math>.<ref name=":17" /> And it follows, as a corollary, that if <math>\varphi \models \neg \psi</math>, then <math>\varphi^D \models \neg \psi^D</math>.<ref name=":17" />

== Conjunctive and disjunctive normal forms ==
{{Main article|Conjunctive normal form|Disjunctive normal form}}
For a formula <math>\varphi</math> in [[disjunctive normal form]], the formula <math>\overline{\varphi}^{D}</math> will be in [[conjunctive normal form]], and given the result that {{section link||Negation is semantically equivalent to dual}}, it will be semantically equivalent to <math>\neg \varphi</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Robinson |first1=Alan J. A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=X3z8ujBRgmEC |title=Handbook of Automated Reasoning |last2=Voronkov |first2=Andrei |date=2001-06-21 |publisher=Gulf Professional Publishing |isbn=978-0-444-82949-8 |pages=306 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Polkowski |first=Lech T. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eO3aEAAAQBAJ |title=Logic: Reference Book for Computer Scientists: The 2nd Revised, Modified, and Enlarged Edition of "Logics for Computer and Data Sciences, and Artificial Intelligence" |date=2023-10-03 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-031-42034-4 |pages=70 |language=en}}</ref> This provides a procedure for converting between conjunctive normal form and disjunctive normal form.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bagdasar |first=Ovidiu |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8lS6BAAAQBAJ |title=Concise Computer Mathematics: Tutorials on Theory and Problems |date=2013-10-28 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-319-01751-8 |pages=36 |language=en}}</ref> Since the [[Disjunctive Normal Form Theorem]] shows that every formula of propositional logic is expressible in disjunctive normal form, every formula is also expressible in conjunctive normal form by means of effecting the conversion to its dual.<ref name=":4" />
